conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: Type 1 (distal) RTA
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: Type 1 (distal) RTA is an inability to secrete H⁺ in the distal tubule → acidosis + alkaline urine, with hypokalaemia and stones.

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: A patient has a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with bicarbonate wasting and other features of Fanconi syndrome (glycosuria, aminoaciduria). Which RTA is this?
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: Type 2 (proximal) RTA
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: Type 2 (proximal) RTA is an inability to reabsorb HCO₃⁻ in the PCT → bicarbonate wasting (part of Fanconi syndrome), with hypokalaemia.

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: Which RTA is characterised by a hyperkalaemic, normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis due to an aldosterone problem?
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: Type 4 RTA
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: Type 4 RTA is aldosterone deficiency/resistance → reduced H⁺ + K⁺ excretion → acidosis + hyperkalaemia — the hyperkalaemic RTA.

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: How do you distinguish a normal-anion-gap from a raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis by mechanism?
options: Normal gap = added acid; raised gap = bicarbonate loss
Normal gap = renal/GI bicarbonate loss (RTA, diarrhoea); raised gap = added acid
Both are caused by bicarbonate loss
Normal gap only occurs in respiratory disorders
Raised gap is always due to diarrhoea
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: Normal gap = renal/GI bicarbonate loss (RTA, diarrhoea); raised gap = added acid
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: Renal or GI bicarbonate loss (RTA, diarrhoea) produces a normal-anion-gap acidosis; added acid produces a raised-anion-gap acidosis.

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: Why is sodium handling essentially equivalent to volume/BP control?
options: Sodium is the main determinant of extracellular volume (water follows sodium), so sodium handling = volume/BP control, distinct from water concentration (ADH)
Sodium is not reabsorbed by the kidney
Sodium is controlled solely by ADH
Sodium has no effect on volume
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: Sodium is the main determinant of extracellular volume (water follows sodium), so sodium handling = volume/BP control, distinct from water concentration (ADH)
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: Sodium is the main determinant of extracellular volume — where sodium goes, water follows — so sodium handling equals volume/BP control. This is distinct from water/concentration control, which is ADH.

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: Which nephron segment reabsorbs the bulk (~65%) of filtered sodium?
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: The proximal convoluted tubule (Na⁺ cotransporters)
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: The PCT reabsorbs ~65% of filtered sodium (bulk) via Na⁺ cotransporters (with glucose/amino acids). The TAL reabsorbs ~25% (NKCC2), DCT ~5% (NCC), and collecting duct ~3% (ENaC, aldosterone-regulated), for ~99% overall.

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: Which step of renal potassium handling is the regulated step that sets K⁺ balance?
options: Reabsorption in the loop of Henle
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: Secretion in the collecting duct
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: K⁺ is filtered, largely reabsorbed proximally, then secreted in the collecting duct — and secretion is the regulated step that sets K⁺ balance.

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: A patient with primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's) would be expected to have which potassium and acid-base abnormality?
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: Hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: Aldosterone retains Na⁺ and excretes K⁺ + H⁺. Excess aldosterone (Conn's) → hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis (and hypertension). Deficiency (Addison's) or K⁺-sparing diuretics → hyperkalaemia.

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: A patient with severe hyperkalaemia is given insulin-dextrose and salbutamol. What is the shared mechanism of these treatments?
options: They shift K⁺ from the blood into cells (insulin and β-agonists drive K⁺ intracellularly)
They stabilise the cardiac membrane directly
They bind K⁺ in the gut
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: They shift K⁺ from the blood into cells (insulin and β-agonists drive K⁺ intracellularly)
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: Insulin, β-agonists (salbutamol) and alkalosis shift K⁺ into cells, lowering plasma K⁺. This is the basis of insulin-dextrose + salbutamol for hyperkalaemia.

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: Which of the following causes potassium to shift OUT of cells, raising plasma K⁺?
options: Acidosis, insulin deficiency (DKA), and cell lysis (tumour lysis, rhabdomyolysis)
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: Acidosis, insulin deficiency (DKA), and cell lysis (tumour lysis, rhabdomyolysis)
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: K⁺ shifts out of cells (↑plasma K⁺) with acidosis, insulin deficiency (DKA), and cell lysis (tumour lysis, rhabdomyolysis). Insulin, β-agonists and alkalosis do the opposite (shift K⁺ in).

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: How do loop and thiazide diuretics affect potassium, and why?
options: They cause hyperkalaemia by blocking distal Na⁺ delivery
They cause hypokalaemia by increasing distal Na⁺ delivery, which increases K⁺ secretion
They have no effect on potassium
They cause hyperkalaemia by blocking aldosterone
They cause hypokalaemia by shifting K⁺ into cells
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: They cause hypokalaemia by increasing distal Na⁺ delivery, which increases K⁺ secretion
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: Loop and thiazide diuretics cause hypokalaemia: increased distal Na⁺ delivery → more Na⁺ reabsorbed distally → more K⁺ exchanged out (↑K⁺ secretion). K⁺-sparing diuretics (spironolactone/amiloride) cause hyperkalaemia instead.

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: Renal calcium reabsorption in the DCT is actively regulated by which hormone?
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: PTH (parathyroid hormone)
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: In the PCT and thick ascending limb, calcium is reabsorbed passively (following Na⁺/water). In the DCT it is actively, regulated reabsorption — PTH-controlled. PTH also increases phosphate excretion and vitamin D activation.

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: A patient with hypercalcaemia is treated with a loop diuretic. Why does this help, in contrast to thiazides?
options: Loop diuretics retain calcium; thiazides lose it
Loop diuretics block NKCC2 → reduce the gradient driving Ca²⁺ reabsorption → lose calcium; thiazides retain calcium (used for stones)
Loop diuretics increase DCT calcium reabsorption
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: Loop diuretics block NKCC2 → reduce the gradient driving Ca²⁺ reabsorption → lose calcium; thiazides retain calcium (used for stones)
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: Loop diuretics block NKCC2 → reduce the gradient driving Ca²⁺ reabsorption → lose calcium (used in hypercalcaemia). Thiazides retain calcium (↑DCT Ca²⁺ reabsorption → ↓urinary Ca²⁺), used to reduce calcium stones and able to cause hypercalcaemia.

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: In CKD, why do patients develop bone disease and secondary hyperparathyroidism?
options: The kidney over-activates vitamin D and excretes phosphate excessively
The failing kidney can't activate vitamin D (1-α-hydroxylase) and retains phosphate → CKD bone disease / secondary hyperparathyroidism
The kidney loses too much calcium in the urine
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: The failing kidney can't activate vitamin D (1-α-hydroxylase) and retains phosphate → CKD bone disease / secondary hyperparathyroidism
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: In CKD, the failing kidney can't activate vitamin D (via 1-α-hydroxylase) and retains phosphate → CKD bone disease / secondary hyperparathyroidism.

conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.question: Why are sodium, potassium and acid-base handling all linked at the collecting duct?
options: Because ADH controls all three there
Because aldosterone drives a single Na⁺-retain / K⁺-and-H⁺-dump exchange in the collecting duct
Because the PCT reabsorbs all three together
Because they share the NKCC2 transporter
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.answer: Because aldosterone drives a single Na⁺-retain / K⁺-and-H⁺-dump exchange in the collecting duct
conditions__RENAL__Foundations of Nephro.explanation: The collecting duct is the fine-tuning hub where aldosterone drives the Na⁺-retain / K⁺-and-H⁺-dump exchange — the conceptual glue linking sodium, potassium and acid-base. Conn's → ↑Na⁺/↓K⁺/↑H⁺ loss (HTN, hypokalaemia, alkalosis); Addison's → the reverse.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: How is CKD defined?
options: A creatinine rise ≥26 µmol/L within 48 h
eGFR <60 or markers of kidney damage (ACR ≥3, haematuria, structural/biopsy abnormality) for >3 months
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: eGFR <60 or markers of kidney damage (ACR ≥3, haematuria, structural/biopsy abnormality) for >3 months
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: CKD = eGFR <60 (or markers of kidney damage — ACR ≥3, haematuria, structural or biopsy abnormality) for >3 months; it is irreversible, progressive nephron loss.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: A patient presents with renal impairment, bilateral small kidneys, anaemia, low calcium and high phosphate. Does this point to AKI or CKD?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Bilateral small kidneys, anaemia (chronic ↓EPO), low calcium, high phosphate and a long-standing history all point to CKD rather than AKI.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: In which condition would the kidneys NOT be small despite CKD?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Kidneys are not small in ADPKD, diabetic nephropathy, HIV and amyloid — these give normal or large kidneys.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: What is the commonest cause of CKD?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of CKD/ESRF, followed by hypertension.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: From what is eGFR estimated?
options: Creatinine, age and sex (UK eGFR is race-free since 2021)
Cystatin C alone in all patients
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: Creatinine, age and sex (UK eGFR is race-free since 2021)
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: UK eGFR (creatinine-based CKD-EPI) is reported from creatinine, age and sex; the Black-ethnicity correction factor was removed in 2021 to give race-free reporting.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: A patient has an eGFR of 50. Which CKD G-stage is this?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Stage 3a is eGFR 45–59 (moderate reduction); 3b is 30–44.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: What eGFR defines CKD stage 5 (established failure)?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Stage 5 is eGFR <15 — established failure requiring dialysis/transplant.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: Why does a normal eGFR alone not equal CKD at stages 1–2?
options: Because staging uses urine output instead
Evidence of kidney damage (e.g. ACR, haematuria) is also required
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: Evidence of kidney damage (e.g. ACR, haematuria) is also required
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Stages 1 (eGFR >90) and 2 (eGFR 60–89) require evidence of kidney damage; a normal eGFR alone is not CKD.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: In the CKD 'heat map', which combination carries the worst prognosis?
options: Low eGFR with A1 ACR only
High eGFR with A3 ACR only
Low eGFR and high ACR together
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: Low eGFR and high ACR together
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: A low eGFR and high ACR together carry the worst prognosis; the ACR axis is what NICE uses for risk (A1 <3, A2 3–30, A3 >30 mg/mmol).

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: Which factor can falsely affect the eGFR?
options: Eating red meat <12 h before the test
Having the sample taken in the afternoon rather than the morning
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: Eating red meat <12 h before the test
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Creatinine-based eGFR can be falsely affected by anything that alters creatinine independently of GFR: eating red meat within ~12 h (transiently raises creatinine → lowers eGFR), and extremes of muscle mass (high muscle mass or creatine supplements raise creatinine; low muscle mass, e.g. cachexia/amputees, lowers it and overestimates GFR). Time of day of the sample does not meaningfully affect it.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: What type of anaemia results from CKD, and by what mechanism?
options: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia from iron loss
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Failing kidneys produce less EPO, causing a normochromic normocytic anaemia (typically once GFR <35).

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: What is a key cardiac consequence of the anaemia of CKD?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: The anaemia of CKD predisposes to left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH).

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: What is the first step in managing the anaemia of CKD before starting an ESA?
options: Transfuse to a high Hb target
Optimise iron (oral, then IV if Hb target not met in 3 months)
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: Optimise iron (oral, then IV if Hb target not met in 3 months)
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Iron is optimised first (oral → IV if the Hb target 10–12 g/dL is not met in 3 months) before starting ESAs (EPO, darbepoetin).

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: Which is a recognised side effect of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in CKD?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: ESA side effects include accelerated HTN, bone aches, flu-like symptoms, rash/urticaria, pure red cell aplasia (anti-EPO antibodies), and raised PCV → thrombosis and functional iron deficiency.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: An ESA is failing to correct the anaemia of CKD. What is the commonest cause?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: ESA failure causes include iron deficiency (commonest), inadequate dose, infection and aluminium toxicity.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: What is the mechanism chain of CKD-mineral bone disease?
options: ↓1-α-hydroxylation of vitamin D + phosphate retention → low calcium → secondary hyperparathyroidism
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: ↓1-α-hydroxylation of vitamin D + phosphate retention → low calcium → secondary hyperparathyroidism
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Reduced 1-α-hydroxylation of vitamin D plus phosphate retention lowers calcium, driving secondary hyperparathyroidism and bone disease.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: A long-standing CKD patient now has a persistently high PTH with a HIGH calcium. What does this represent?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: After long-standing secondary disease, the glands become autonomous (tertiary hyperparathyroidism): PTH stays high with a high calcium, and parathyroidectomy may be needed.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: What is the first step in managing CKD-mineral bone disease?
options: Start a phosphate binder before dietary measures
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: The ladder is: reduce dietary phosphate (1st) → phosphate binders (sevelamer) → activated vitamin D (alfacalcidol, calcitriol) → cinacalcet if hyperPTH persists.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: Which phosphate binder is named for CKD-mineral bone disease management?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Sevelamer is the phosphate binder; cinacalcet is added if hyperPTH persists and alfacalcidol/calcitriol are the activated vitamin D agents.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: Which urine sample is used to measure ACR in CKD?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: ACR is the proteinuria marker, measured on a first-pass early-morning urine sample.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: An initial ACR is 50 mg/mmol. What is the next step?
options: Repeat on a second early-morning sample to confirm
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: Repeat on a second early-morning sample to confirm
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: ACR 3–70 should be repeated on a second early-morning sample to confirm; ACR >70 needs no repeat.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: What is the treatment of proteinuria in CKD?
options: ACE inhibitor (at ACR >30 with HTN, or >70 regardless) + SGLT2 inhibitor
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: ACE inhibitor (at ACR >30 with HTN, or >70 regardless) + SGLT2 inhibitor
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Proteinuria is treated with an ACE inhibitor (ACR >30 with HTN, or >70 regardless) plus an SGLT2 inhibitor for added renoprotection.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: What is the leading cause of death in CKD, and what does this mandate?
options: Cardiovascular disease — statin for all CKD patients
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: Cardiovascular disease — statin for all CKD patients
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: CVD is the leading cause of death in CKD, so a statin is given to all CKD patients.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: How is the metabolic acidosis of CKD treated?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Metabolic acidosis in CKD is treated with oral sodium bicarbonate; hyperkalaemia with dietary K+ restriction and fluid overload with salt/fluid restriction and loop diuretics.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: What is the first-line renoprotective drug for slowing CKD progression?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: An ACE inhibitor is first-line and renoprotective in CKD.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: After starting an ACE inhibitor in CKD, the creatinine rises by 25%. What is the appropriate action?
options: Stop immediately and investigate for renal artery stenosis
Halve the dose and recheck in a year
Continue — a rise up to 30% (eGFR fall up to 25%) is acceptable
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: Continue — a rise up to 30% (eGFR fall up to 25%) is acceptable
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: A creatinine rise up to 30% (or eGFR fall up to 25%) is acceptable after starting an ACE inhibitor; beyond that, stop and investigate for renal artery stenosis.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: A creatinine rises by 40% after starting an ACE inhibitor in CKD. What does this suggest and what should be done?
options: Stop and investigate for renal artery stenosis
Continue, as any rise is expected
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: Stop and investigate for renal artery stenosis
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: A rise beyond 30% (eGFR fall beyond 25%) is not acceptable — stop the ACE inhibitor and investigate for renal artery stenosis.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: In which CKD group are SGLT2 inhibitors particularly useful for slowing progression?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors slow progression, especially in diabetic/proteinuric CKD.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: Where do loop diuretics act, and do they work at low eGFR?
options: Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal tubule; lose efficacy at low eGFR
Collecting duct aldosterone receptor; ineffective in CKD
Proximal tubule carbonic anhydrase; only work at high eGFR
Glomerulus directly; work only above eGFR 60
Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb; still work at low eGFR
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb; still work at low eGFR
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Loop diuretics (furosemide) block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb and still work at low eGFR, useful for fluid overload.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: Thiazide diuretics act on which transporter and have what limitation in CKD?
options: Na-K-2Cl cotransporter; still effective at any eGFR
Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal tubule; lose efficacy once eGFR <30
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.answer: Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal tubule; lose efficacy once eGFR <30
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Thiazides block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal tubule (used for BP) but lose efficacy once eGFR <30.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: Which finding warrants referral to nephrology in CKD?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Refer if eGFR <30 (stage 4–5); ACR ≥70; ACR ≥30 with haematuria; sustained eGFR fall ≥25% (+ stage change) or ≥15 mL/min/year; poorly controlled HTN on ≥4 agents; or a suspected genetic/rare cause.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: What treatment is required at CKD stage 5?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: Stage 5 (eGFR <15) is established failure requiring renal replacement therapy — dialysis or transplant.

conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.question: Which vaccinations should be offered to CKD patients alongside avoiding nephrotoxics?
conditions__RENAL__Chronic Kidney Diseas.explanation: CKD management includes avoiding nephrotoxics (NSAIDs), dose-adjusting renally excreted drugs, and offering influenza + pneumococcal vaccination.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What is the 'decisive fork' that underlies almost every glomerular question?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: The decisive fork is nephritic (filter inflamed and bleeding → blood + cells in urine) vs nephrotic (barrier broken → massive protein loss).

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: Which set of features is the 'gestalt' of nephritic syndrome?
options: Heavy proteinuria + normal BP + marked oedema
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Nephritic = haematuria + HTN + oliguria (an inflamed, bleeding glomerulus); nephrotic = proteinuria + hypoalbuminaemia + oedema.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: Which casts are characteristic of nephritic syndrome?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Red cell casts characterise nephritic syndrome; fatty/oval bodies are seen in nephrotic syndrome.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What level of proteinuria defines the nephrotic range?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Nephrotic-range proteinuria is heavy (>3 g/day); nephritic proteinuria is mild–moderate (<3 g).

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What is the diagnostic triad of nephrotic syndrome?
options: Proteinuria >3 g/24 h, hypoalbuminaemia <30 g/L, oedema
Red cell casts, low C3, raised ASO
Proteinuria <3 g, normal albumin, no oedema
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.answer: Proteinuria >3 g/24 h, hypoalbuminaemia <30 g/L, oedema
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: The nephrotic triad is proteinuria >3 g/24 h, hypoalbuminaemia <30 g/L, and oedema (periorbital, peripheral).

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: Why are patients with nephrotic syndrome hypercoagulable?
options: Loss of clotting factors causing bleeding
Urinary loss of antithrombin III, protein C & S plus raised fibrinogen
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.answer: Urinary loss of antithrombin III, protein C & S plus raised fibrinogen
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Urinary loss of antithrombin III, protein C & S plus raised fibrinogen makes nephrotic patients hypercoagulable; VTE is the big complication.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: Why are nephrotic patients prone to infection, especially with encapsulated organisms?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Urinary IgG loss leaves nephrotic patients susceptible to infection, especially with encapsulated organisms.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: Which mechanism explains hypocalcaemia in nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Loss of vitamin-D-binding protein in the urine causes hypocalcaemia in nephrotic syndrome.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What is the general (non-disease-specific) management of nephrotic syndrome?
options: ACEi/ARB, loop diuretic + salt restriction, statin, anticoagulation if high VTE risk, pneumococcal vaccination
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.answer: ACEi/ARB, loop diuretic + salt restriction, statin, anticoagulation if high VTE risk, pneumococcal vaccination
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: General nephrotic management is ACEi/ARB (reduce proteinuria), loop diuretic + salt restriction (oedema), statin (hyperlipidaemia), anticoagulation if high VTE risk/very low albumin, and pneumococcal vaccination — plus disease-specific therapy.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What are the three classic nephrotic diseases?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: The three classic nephrotic diseases are minimal change (kids), FSGS, and membranous (adults).

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: Which test is the definitive investigation in glomerulonephritis, and how is it reported?
options: Urine dipstick — blood and protein only
Renal biopsy — light microscopy, electron microscopy, immunofluorescence
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.answer: Renal biopsy — light microscopy, electron microscopy, immunofluorescence
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Renal biopsy is definitive, reported three ways: light microscopy (architecture), electron microscopy (ultrastructure), and immunofluorescence (deposits + pattern).

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: A child develops nephritic syndrome 10 days after a sore throat, with a raised ASO titre and low C3. Which diagnosis fits?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Nephritic syndrome 7–14 days after a group A strep infection with a raised ASO titre and low C3 is post-streptococcal GN.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: A positive anti-PLA2R antibody points to which glomerular disease?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Anti-PLA2R antibodies point to membranous nephropathy on the serology discriminator.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: Which biopsy picture is characteristic of minimal change disease?
options: Thickened BM with spike and dome, granular IgG/C3
Crescents with linear IgG along the BM
Normal light microscopy, foot-process effacement on EM, negative immunofluorescence
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.answer: Normal light microscopy, foot-process effacement on EM, negative immunofluorescence
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Minimal change disease shows normal light microscopy (hence the name), foot-process effacement on EM, and negative immunofluorescence.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: A 4-year-old presents with pure nephrotic syndrome and a normal renal biopsy on light microscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis and key treatment feature?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: A child with pure nephrotic syndrome and normal light microscopy has minimal change disease, which is highly steroid-responsive (the defining feature) with an excellent prognosis.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What type of proteinuria occurs in minimal change disease, and why?
options: Non-selective with all plasma proteins lost
Selective (albumin only) due to increased GBM permeability to albumin
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.answer: Selective (albumin only) due to increased GBM permeability to albumin
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: T-cell + cytokine-mediated GBM damage increases permeability to albumin, causing selective proteinuria (albumin only).

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: A patient with HIV develops nephrotic syndrome; biopsy shows focal segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: FSGS is associated with HIV, heroin and sickle cell; biopsy shows focal (some glomeruli) and segmental (part of each) sclerosis + hyalinosis.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: Compared with minimal change disease, FSGS is characterised by which feature?
options: Higher steroid-resistance and recurrence in transplants
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.answer: Higher steroid-resistance and recurrence in transplants
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: FSGS has higher steroid-resistance and a higher recurrence rate in transplants than minimal change disease, and is a cause of CKD.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: An older Caucasian adult presents with nephrotic syndrome; biopsy EM shows subepithelial deposits with a 'spike and dome' appearance. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Membranous nephropathy is the commonest nephrotic syndrome in older Caucasian adults; EM shows subepithelial deposits ('spike and dome') with granular IgG/C3 on IF.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: Which nephrotic disease carries the highest VTE risk and follows a 'rule of thirds'?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Membranous nephropathy carries the highest VTE risk of the nephrotics and follows a rule of thirds (⅓ remit, ⅓ stable, ⅓ progress).

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What is the named immunosuppressive regimen for progressive membranous nephropathy?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Progressive membranous nephropathy is treated with the Ponticelli regimen (corticosteroids + cyclophosphamide); ACEi/ARB is used for all to reduce proteinuria.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What is the commonest cause of glomerulonephritis worldwide?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) is the commonest cause of glomerulonephritis worldwide.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: A young man develops visible haematuria 1–2 days after a URTI. Which diagnosis is most likely, and what distinguishes it from post-strep GN?
options: IgA nephropathy — haematuria 1–2 days post-URTI vs post-strep at 1–2 weeks
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.answer: IgA nephropathy — haematuria 1–2 days post-URTI vs post-strep at 1–2 weeks
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Haematuria 1–2 days after a URTI in a young person is IgA nephropathy; the short interval distinguishes it from post-strep GN (1–2 weeks).

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What is the immunofluorescence finding in IgA nephropathy?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA on immunofluorescence, reflecting mesangial deposition of IgA immune complexes.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: An IgA nephropathy patient has persistent proteinuria >0.5–1 g/day. What is the appropriate treatment?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: In IgA nephropathy, isolated haematuria with normal eGFR and proteinuria <1 g/day is monitored; persistent proteinuria >0.5–1 g warrants an ACE inhibitor; active disease/no ACEi response → corticosteroids.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What is the time interval from group A strep infection to post-streptococcal GN?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Post-streptococcal GN develops 7–14 days after a group A strep infection (throat or skin), mostly in children.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: Which biopsy findings are characteristic of post-streptococcal GN?
options: Spike and dome with granular IgG/C3
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Post-strep GN shows endothelial/neutrophilic proliferation, subepithelial 'humps' on EM, and a 'starry sky' IgG/IgM/C3 pattern on IF.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What is the management and prognosis of post-streptococcal GN in children?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Post-strep GN is managed supportively (BP control, fluid/salt management, treat residual infection); most children recover fully with a good prognosis.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: A man presents with haemoptysis and nephritis; renal biopsy shows linear IgG along the basement membrane. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Pulmonary haemorrhage + nephritis with linear IgG along the basement membrane is anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture's), caused by anti-GBM antibodies against type IV collagen.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What is the management of anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture's)?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Anti-GBM disease is treated with plasmapheresis (to remove antibodies) plus corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: How does GPA (Wegener's) differ from anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture's)?
options: GPA has linear IgG; Goodpasture's has crescents
GPA is anti-GBM positive; Goodpasture's is ANCA positive
GPA adds upper-airway features (wheeze, saddle-nose deformity, sinusitis) and is ANCA-positive
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.answer: GPA adds upper-airway features (wheeze, saddle-nose deformity, sinusitis) and is ANCA-positive
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: GPA (Wegener's) adds upper-airway features and is ANCA-positive; c-ANCA/PR3 = GPA and p-ANCA/MPO = microscopic polyangiitis, the anti-GBM differential.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: A child develops a palpable purpuric rash on the buttocks and legs, abdominal pain, polyarthritis and haematuria after an infection. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: The HSP tetrad is a palpable purpuric rash (extensor surfaces of buttocks + legs), abdominal pain, polyarthritis and IgA nephropathy — an IgA-mediated vasculitis and the systemic cousin of IgA nephropathy.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What is the management of Henoch-Schönlein purpura?
options: Supportive (self-limiting) with analgesia; monitor BP + urinalysis
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.answer: Supportive (self-limiting) with analgesia; monitor BP + urinalysis
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: HSP is usually self-limiting; management is supportive with analgesia for arthralgia and monitoring of BP + urinalysis for renal involvement.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What characterises rapidly progressive (crescentic) GN?
options: Isolated microscopic haematuria with normal function
Nephritic syndrome with rapid loss of renal function over days–weeks; a nephrological emergency
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.answer: Nephritic syndrome with rapid loss of renal function over days–weeks; a nephrological emergency
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: RPGN is a pattern — nephritic syndrome with rapid loss of renal function over days–weeks — and is a nephrological emergency.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What is the characteristic biopsy finding in rapidly progressive GN?
options: Crescents in the glomeruli (proliferating cells filling Bowman's space)
Foot-process effacement with normal light microscopy
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.answer: Crescents in the glomeruli (proliferating cells filling Bowman's space)
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: RPGN shows crescents in the glomeruli (proliferating cells filling Bowman's space); causes include anti-GBM, ANCA-associated, and severe post-strep/lupus nephritis.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: What is the management of rapidly progressive (crescentic) GN?
options: Aggressive immunosuppression — high-dose steroids + cyclophosphamide ± plasmapheresis
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.answer: Aggressive immunosuppression — high-dose steroids + cyclophosphamide ± plasmapheresis
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: RPGN is treated urgently with aggressive immunosuppression — high-dose steroids + cyclophosphamide ± plasmapheresis.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: A low C3 with a raised ASO titre most specifically points to which diagnosis?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Low C3 occurs in post-streptococcal and membranoproliferative GN, but a raised ASO titre specifically indicates post-streptococcal GN.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: Which secondary association is recognised for minimal change disease?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Minimal change disease is mostly idiopathic but has secondary associations including NSAIDs, rifampicin, Hodgkin's lymphoma, thymoma and infectious mononucleosis.

conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.question: Which secondary cause is classically associated with membranous nephropathy?
conditions__RENAL__Glomerulonephritis (n.explanation: Membranous nephropathy has secondary causes including hepatitis B, malaria, malignancy (solid tumours — paraneoplastic), penicillamine/NSAIDs/gold, SLE, thyroiditis and RA.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: A renal section shows numerous rounded tufts of capillaries surrounded by a space, plus many convoluted tubules. This region is the:
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: Renal corpuscles (glomerular tufts) are found only in the cortex, along with the convoluted tubules; the medulla has only straight tubules and vessels.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: The striated appearance of the renal medulla is due to:
options: Parallel straight tubules (loops of Henle, collecting ducts) and vasa recta
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: The medulla contains parallel straight tubules and vasa recta running in the same direction, giving a striated look; it contains no glomeruli.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: Cortical tissue extending down between the renal pyramids is called the:
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: Columns of Bertin are cortical extensions between pyramids; medullary rays are straight tubules within the cortex.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: Which nephrons are chiefly responsible for producing concentrated urine?
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops of Henle and vasa recta that establish the medullary osmotic gradient needed to concentrate urine.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: On H&E, a cortical tubule that is intensely eosinophilic with a brush border, a narrow fuzzy lumen and few nuclei per cross-section is the:
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: The PCT is eosinophilic (mitochondria-rich) with an apical brush border, a narrow lumen and few nuclei per profile; the DCT is paler with a clear lumen and more nuclei.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: Which sequence correctly lists the collecting/drainage pathway?
options: Collecting duct -> papillary duct -> minor calyx -> major calyx -> renal pelvis -> ureter
Collecting duct -> major calyx -> minor calyx -> pelvis -> ureter
Papillary duct -> collecting duct -> pelvis -> calyx -> ureter
Minor calyx -> collecting duct -> major calyx -> ureter
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: Urine passes collecting ducts -> papillary ducts of Bellini -> minor calyx -> major calyx -> renal pelvis -> ureter.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: The two principal cell types of the collecting duct and their roles are:
options: Principal cells (ADH/aquaporins, Na/K) and intercalated cells (acid-base)
Type I and type II cells
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: Principal cells respond to ADH via aquaporins and handle Na+/K+; intercalated cells regulate acid-base balance.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: The epithelium lining the minor calyces, renal pelvis and ureter is:
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: The pelvicalyceal system and ureter are lined by urothelium (transitional epithelium), which is the site of urothelial carcinoma.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: A renal lobe is defined as:
options: A medullary ray plus surrounding cortex
One pyramid plus its overlying cortex
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: A renal lobe = one medullary pyramid plus the cortex capping it; a lobule is a medullary ray plus its surrounding cortex.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: Erythropoietin, renin and activation of vitamin D reflect which kidney function?
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: These are the kidney's endocrine functions: EPO (red-cell production), renin (BP/volume) and 1-alpha-hydroxylase (active vitamin D).

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: Renal papillary necrosis is classically associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: Papillary necrosis is linked to diabetes, analgesic nephropathy, sickle cell disease and obstruction/pyelonephritis (mnemonic POSTCARDS); minimal change disease is a glomerular (podocyte) disorder, not a cause.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: Renal cell carcinoma most commonly arises from and forms a mass in the:
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: Renal cell carcinoma arises from renal tubular epithelium, presenting as a cortical mass; urothelial carcinoma arises from the pelvicalyceal urothelium.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: Which structure marks where the distal tubule contacts its parent glomerulus?
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: The early distal tubule returns to the vascular pole of its own corpuscle as the macula densa, part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: Which stain is most useful for assessing basement membranes and the brush border in a renal biopsy?
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: PAS highlights basement membranes and the PCT brush border and is a routine part of renal biopsy assessment; silver stains the GBM/mesangium.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: Acute tubular necrosis, the commonest cause of intrinsic AKI, primarily injures the:
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: ATN is injury to tubular epithelial cells (especially PCT and thick ascending limb) from ischaemia or toxins.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: Dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces from obstructed outflow is termed:
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: Hydronephrosis is pelvicalyceal dilatation due to obstruction, which can atrophy the parenchyma if unrelieved.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: Collecting ducts are best distinguished from convoluted tubules by:
options: Pale cytoplasm with sharply defined cell borders
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: Collecting ducts have pale cytoplasm and distinct (sharp) cell borders, unlike the eosinophilic PCT or paler DCT; they run through medulla and medullary rays.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: Approximately what proportion of nephrons are juxtamedullary?
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: About 15% of nephrons are juxtamedullary (long-looped, concentrating), while ~85% are cortical.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: The renal medulla is especially vulnerable to ischaemic injury (ATN, papillary necrosis) because it:
options: Receives little blood flow and works at low oxygen tension while doing active transport
Is supplied only by the hepatic artery
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: Although the kidneys take ~20-25% of cardiac output, ~90% perfuses the cortex; the medulla runs at low pO2 while performing energy-demanding solute transport, making it the ischaemic watershed for ATN and papillary necrosis.

histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.question: The loop of Henle acts as the countercurrent ______ and the vasa recta as the countercurrent ______.
histology__RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medull.explanation: The loop of Henle is the countercurrent multiplier that builds the medullary osmotic gradient (~300->1200 mOsm); the vasa recta are the countercurrent exchanger that preserves it.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: Which sequence correctly describes the layers crossed by filtrate in the glomerulus?
options: Fenestrated endothelium -> glomerular basement membrane -> podocyte slit diaphragm
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Filtrate crosses the fenestrated endothelium, then the GBM, then the podocyte slit diaphragm — providing size and charge selectivity.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: The negative charge of the filtration barrier that repels albumin is provided mainly by:
options: Heparan sulfate proteoglycans in the GBM
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Heparan sulfate proteoglycans in the GBM give the anionic charge that repels negatively charged proteins such as albumin.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: A child has nephrotic syndrome; light microscopy and immunofluorescence are normal, but EM shows diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement. The diagnosis is:
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Normal LM/IF with foot-process effacement on EM in a child with nephrotic syndrome is minimal change disease (typically steroid-responsive).

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: The slit diaphragm between podocyte foot processes depends on which proteins?
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Nephrin and podocin (with CD2AP) are essential slit-diaphragm proteins; their mutation causes congenital nephrotic syndrome.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: Which cell in the glomerulus is contractile and helps regulate GFR while also being phagocytic?
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Mesangial cells support the loops, contract to modulate capillary surface area/GFR, phagocytose trapped material, and secrete matrix/cytokines.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: At the vascular pole of the renal corpuscle:
options: A single artery enters and a vein leaves
The afferent arteriole enters and the efferent arteriole leaves
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: The vascular pole is where the afferent arteriole enters and efferent arteriole leaves; filtrate exits at the opposite urinary pole into the PCT.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: Membranous nephropathy characteristically shows on EM and silver stain:
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Membranous nephropathy has subepithelial immune deposits with intervening GBM 'spikes' on silver stain and granular IF (often anti-PLA2R).

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: Linear immunofluorescence along the GBM is characteristic of:
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Linear IF reflects anti-GBM antibodies (Goodpasture); immune-complex diseases give granular IF.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: Nodular mesangial expansion known as Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules is seen in:
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules are the nodular glomerulosclerosis of diabetic nephropathy, with GBM thickening.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: The fenestrated glomerular endothelium primarily prevents passage of:
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: The endothelial fenestrae (~70-100 nm) allow plasma through but retain cellular blood elements.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: Which finding on immunofluorescence suggests immune-complex-mediated disease rather than anti-GBM disease?
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Granular ('lumpy-bumpy') deposits indicate immune-complex deposition (e.g. lupus, PSGN); linear staining indicates anti-GBM antibody.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: The commonest primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, with mesangial IgA deposits and haematuria, is:
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: IgA nephropathy is the commonest primary GN, characterised by mesangial IgA deposition and episodic haematuria (often 1-2 days after an upper respiratory infection).

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: Which statement about podocytes is correct?
options: They line the outer wall of Bowman's capsule
They are terminally differentiated and their loss is often irreversible
They have interdigitating foot processes bridged by slit diaphragms and divide readily
They are contractile and regulate GFR
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Podocytes are terminally differentiated visceral epithelial cells with foot processes and slit diaphragms; they divide poorly, so their loss tends to be irreversible.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: A split, basketweave GBM on EM with haematuria and sensorineural deafness suggests:
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Alport syndrome is a type IV collagen defect producing a lamellated/basketweave GBM with haematuria, deafness and ocular signs.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: Much of the filtration barrier's negative (charge) selectivity comes from heparan sulfate in the:
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Heparan sulfate proteoglycans in the GBM (with the endothelial glycocalyx) provide much of the charge barrier; size selectivity is shared, with the podocyte slit diaphragm the major size sieve.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: Nephrotic-range proteinuria in glomerular disease most directly reflects injury to the:
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Heavy proteinuria results from disruption of the podocyte/GBM charge barrier (the nephrotic mechanism).

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: Congenital (Finnish-type) nephrotic syndrome is caused by mutation in the gene encoding:
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type is due to NPHS1 mutations affecting nephrin, a core slit-diaphragm protein.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: On a renal biopsy, 'tram-tracking' or double contours of the GBM on silver stain suggests:
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Double contours/tram-tracking of the GBM (from subendothelial deposits and mesangial interposition) are characteristic of MPGN.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: Which glomerular structure is continuous with the lumen of the proximal convoluted tubule?
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Bowman's space at the urinary pole drains directly into the PCT lumen.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: The nephritic syndrome (haematuria, red-cell casts, hypertension) reflects predominant injury to which glomerular compartment?
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Nephritic syndrome arises from endothelial/mesangial inflammation with GBM breaks allowing red cells into the urine; podocyte/charge injury gives the nephrotic picture.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: An ACE inhibitor acutely lowers GFR mainly by:
options: Dilating the efferent arteriole and reducing glomerular hydrostatic pressure
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole; ACE inhibitors/ARBs dilate it, lowering glomerular capillary pressure and GFR - renoprotective long-term but hazardous in bilateral renal artery stenosis.

histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.question: The commonest cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults, showing segmental scarring of some glomeruli with HIV and obesity associations, is:
histology__RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtratio.explanation: FSGS shows focal, segmental glomerulosclerosis with foot-process effacement; it is the commonest primary adult nephrotic syndrome (esp. Black patients, APOL1) and is associated with HIV, heroin, obesity and reduced nephron mass.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: A cortical tubule is intensely eosinophilic with a prominent brush border, a fuzzy narrow lumen and only a few nuclei per cross-section. It is the:
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Brush border, eosinophilia, fuzzy narrow lumen and few nuclei per profile identify the PCT.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: The thick ascending limb of Henle is called the 'diluting segment' because it:
options: Actively reabsorbs NaCl (NKCC2) while being impermeable to water
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: The TAL pumps out NaCl via NKCC2 but is water-impermeable, so it dilutes the tubular fluid and builds the medullary gradient.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Loop diuretics such as furosemide act on which transporter and segment?
options: NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Loop diuretics inhibit NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Thiazide diuretics act on which transporter?
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Thiazides block the NCC cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct by:
options: Inserting aquaporin-2 channels into principal cells
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: ADH inserts aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane of principal cells, allowing water reabsorption down the medullary gradient.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: A patient has glucosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia and a proximal renal tubular acidosis. This indicates dysfunction of the:
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Generalised PCT transport failure (Fanconi syndrome) causes loss of glucose, amino acids, phosphate and bicarbonate in the urine.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Which cell of the collecting duct secretes H+ and reabsorbs bicarbonate?
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Alpha-intercalated cells secrete H+ (and reabsorb HCO3-); beta-intercalated cells secrete bicarbonate.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: An inherited defect producing a thiazide-like picture (hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalciuria) localises to the:
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Gitelman syndrome is a DCT NCC defect that mimics chronic thiazide use.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: The thin descending limb of Henle is permeable to:
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: The thin descending limb is water-permeable (AQP1) but solute-impermeable, so the tubular fluid concentrates as it descends.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: A gain-of-function mutation of ENaC causing hypertension and hypokalaemia with low aldosterone is:
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Liddle syndrome is constitutive ENaC activation in the collecting duct, causing Na+ retention, hypertension and hypokalaemia despite low aldosterone.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Muddy-brown granular casts in the urine are characteristic of:
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Muddy-brown granular casts of sloughed tubular cells are the classic urinary finding in acute tubular necrosis.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Which tubule reabsorbs all of the filtered glucose, and via which transporter?
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Essentially all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT via SGLT2 (and SGLT1); SGLT2 inhibitors block this.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Acetazolamide (a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) acts primarily at the:
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors block bicarbonate reabsorption in the PCT.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Which segment contributes the macula densa of the juxtaglomerular apparatus?
options: Terminal thick ascending limb (at the TAL-DCT junction)
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: The macula densa is a specialised plaque at the end of the thick ascending limb, where it abuts the vascular pole of its own glomerulus and senses tubular NaCl (older texts loosely call it early distal tubule).

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Spironolactone exerts its diuretic effect by:
options: Blocking the aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) receptor in the collecting duct
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Spironolactone antagonises the aldosterone receptor in collecting-duct principal cells (potassium-sparing); amiloride blocks ENaC directly.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Which statement about the DCT is correct?
options: It has a prominent brush border
It reabsorbs Ca2+ under PTH control and uses NCC for NaCl
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: The DCT lacks a brush border, reabsorbs NaCl via NCC (thiazide-sensitive) and reabsorbs calcium under PTH control.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus results from:
options: Loss of the PCT brush border
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Nephrogenic DI is renal unresponsiveness to ADH (V2 receptor or aquaporin-2 defect), producing dilute urine; central DI is ADH deficiency.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Which limb of the loop of Henle is water-impermeable and actively transports salt?
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs NaCl via NKCC2 and is impermeable to water (the diluting segment).

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: A defect of thick-ascending-limb transport producing a loop-diuretic-like picture with hypercalciuria is:
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Bartter syndrome is a TAL/NKCC2 defect (loop-diuretic-like), with hypokalaemic alkalosis and hypercalciuria; Gitelman (DCT) causes hypocalciuria.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis results from a defect in which collecting-duct cell?
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Type 1 (distal) RTA reflects failure of H+ secretion by alpha-intercalated cells of the collecting duct.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Which renal tubular acidosis is characteristically HYPERkalaemic?
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: Type 4 RTA results from hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance, impairing distal Na+/K+ exchange and causing a hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis; types 1 and 2 are hypokalaemic.

histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.question: Loop diuretics cause hypercalciuria because blocking NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb:
options: Abolishes the lumen-positive voltage that drives paracellular Ca2+ reabsorption
histology__RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of.explanation: NKCC2 activity, with ROMK recycling K+ into the lumen, generates a lumen-positive voltage that drives paracellular Ca2+/Mg2+ reabsorption; loop diuretics abolish it, raising calcium excretion (useful in hypercalcaemia). Thiazides, acting distally, instead cause hypocalciuria.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: The macula densa is a specialised part of which structure, and what does it sense?
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: The macula densa is modified distal-tubule epithelium that senses the NaCl (chloride) concentration of the fluid delivered to the distal tubule.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: Renin is secreted by which cells of the JGA?
options: Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells of the afferent arteriole
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: Renin is produced by the juxtaglomerular (granular) cells — modified smooth muscle of the afferent arteriole.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: Which of the following is NOT a trigger for renin release?
options: Increased NaCl delivery to the distal tubule
Decreased NaCl at the macula densa
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: Increased distal NaCl delivery SUPPRESSES renin. Renin is stimulated by low perfusion (baroreceptor), low macula-densa NaCl, sympathetic beta-1 activity and volume depletion.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts which arteriole, and what is the effect on GFR?
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole, raising glomerular capillary pressure and helping maintain GFR when perfusion is low.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: A patient with bilateral renal artery stenosis is started on an ACE inhibitor and develops acute kidney injury. The mechanism is:
options: Loss of angiotensin II-mediated efferent constriction, dropping glomerular pressure
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: In bilateral RAS, GFR depends on angiotensin II-driven efferent constriction; ACE inhibition removes it, lowering glomerular pressure and precipitating AKI.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: In tubuloglomerular feedback, a high GFR increases NaCl at the macula densa, which responds by releasing:
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: High distal NaCl triggers macula-densa adenosine release, constricting the afferent arteriole to lower GFR (autoregulation).

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: Angiotensin-converting enzyme is located predominantly in the:
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: ACE, which converts angiotensin I to II, is found mainly on lung capillary endothelium.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: Which three cells/structures make up the juxtaglomerular apparatus?
options: Macula densa, juxtaglomerular (granular) cells, extraglomerular mesangial cells
Principal, intercalated, and macula densa cells
Afferent arteriole, efferent arteriole, vasa recta
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: The JGA comprises the macula densa (DCT), the granular (renin) cells of the afferent arteriole, and the extraglomerular mesangial cells.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: NSAIDs can reduce GFR because they:
options: Block prostaglandins that dilate the afferent arteriole
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit vasodilator prostaglandins on the afferent arteriole; without them the afferent constricts and GFR falls, especially in hypovolaemia.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: A young patient has hypertension, hypokalaemia and markedly elevated plasma renin and aldosterone, with a small renal mass. The likely diagnosis is:
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: A renin-secreting JG-cell tumour (reninoma) drives high renin and aldosterone, causing hypertension with hypokalaemia.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: Which cell type acts as an intrarenal baroreceptor for perfusion pressure?
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: The granular (JG) cells sense afferent arteriolar stretch/pressure; reduced stretch increases renin secretion.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: Which memory hook correctly links drugs to arterioles?
options: NSAIDs act on the efferent; ACE inhibitors on the afferent
NSAIDs act on the afferent; ACE inhibitors on the efferent
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: A-fferent = NSAIDs (prostaglandin-mediated dilation); E-fferent = ACE inhibitors (angiotensin II-mediated constriction).

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: Renin acts on which substrate to begin the RAAS cascade?
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: Renin cleaves liver-derived angiotensinogen to angiotensin I.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: The extraglomerular mesangial cells of the JGA are thought mainly to:
options: Bridge and relay signals between the macula densa and arterioles
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: Extraglomerular mesangial (lacis) cells connect the macula densa and arterioles and relay signals via gap junctions.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: Which change would increase GFR?
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: Efferent constriction (or afferent dilation) raises glomerular capillary pressure and increases GFR; afferent constriction lowers it.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: Beta-blockers lower blood pressure partly by acting on the JGA to:
options: Decrease renin release (blocking beta-1 stimulation of JG cells)
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: Beta-1 blockade reduces sympathetic stimulation of JG cells, decreasing renin secretion and RAAS activity.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: Aldosterone, released as part of the RAAS, acts on the kidney to:
options: Increase Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion in the collecting duct
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: Angiotensin II stimulates adrenal aldosterone, which increases Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion via collecting-duct principal cells, expanding volume.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: Renovascular hypertension from unilateral renal artery stenosis is driven by:
options: Reduced renal perfusion increasing renin release
Excess aldosterone from an adrenal adenoma
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: Stenosis lowers perfusion to the affected kidney, stimulating renin release and RAAS-mediated hypertension.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: A patient develops a persistent dry cough on an ACE inhibitor. The mechanism, and the best alternative drug, are:
options: Excess angiotensin II; switch to a beta-blocker
Low aldosterone; switch to a thiazide
Accumulation of bradykinin; switch to an ARB
Efferent dilation; switch to an NSAID
Renin excess; switch to a loop diuretic
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: ACE (kininase II) normally degrades bradykinin; ACE inhibitors raise it, causing cough and angioedema. An ARB blocks the AT1 receptor without raising bradykinin, so it is the usual substitute.

histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.question: SGLT2 inhibitors are renoprotective partly because increasing NaCl delivery to the macula densa causes:
options: Tubuloglomerular-feedback afferent constriction, lowering intraglomerular pressure
histology__RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Appara.explanation: By blocking proximal Na/glucose reabsorption, SGLT2 inhibitors raise macula densa NaCl; tubuloglomerular feedback then constricts the afferent arteriole, reducing glomerular hyperfiltration pressure and slowing CKD progression.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: A tubular organ shows a star-shaped lumen lined by an epithelium with dome-shaped superficial cells, surrounded by inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle. This is the:
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: A star-shaped urothelial lumen with inner-longitudinal/outer-circular muscle (opposite of gut) is characteristic of the ureter.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: The impermeability of the urothelial barrier depends chiefly on umbrella cells' :
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: Umbrella cells have uroplakin-containing asymmetric unit membrane plaques plus tight junctions, forming the blood-urine barrier.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: As the bladder fills, the urothelium:
options: Increases its number of apparent cell layers
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: On distension the cells flatten and slide over one another, so the urothelium appears to have fewer layers (2-3 vs 5-6 when relaxed).

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: The ureteric muscular arrangement differs from the gut in that it is:
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: The ureter has inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle, the reverse of the gastrointestinal tract.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: A renal stone causing loin-to-groin colic is most likely to impact at which sites?
options: The pelviureteric junction, pelvic brim (iliac vessels) and vesicoureteric junction
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: The three ureteric constrictions — PUJ, pelvic brim, and VUJ — are the classic sites of stone impaction.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: Detrusor contraction to empty the bladder is mediated by:
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: Parasympathetic (pelvic nerve) stimulation of M3 muscarinic receptors contracts the detrusor for voiding.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: Painless haematuria in a smoker, with CK7/CK20/uroplakin-positive tumour cells, indicates:
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: Urothelial carcinoma is the commonest bladder cancer, presents with painless haematuria, is linked to smoking/aniline dyes and expresses urothelial markers (CK7/CK20/uroplakin).

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: Chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection of the bladder predisposes to which cancer?
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: Schistosomiasis causes chronic irritation with squamous metaplasia, predisposing to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: The oblique passage of the ureter through the bladder wall functions to:
options: Act as a one-way anti-reflux valve
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: The oblique vesicoureteric junction acts as a valve preventing reflux of urine up the ureter during bladder filling/voiding.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: Which large superficial urothelial cell, often binucleate, is diagnostic of urothelium?
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: Umbrella (superficial) cells are the large, dome-shaped, often binucleate cells defining urothelium.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: The bladder trigone differs from the rest of the bladder mucosa in that it is:
options: Thrown into rugae when the bladder is empty
Smooth (flat) even when the bladder is empty
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: The trigone is a smooth, flat triangle between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral opening; unlike the rest of the bladder it lacks rugae. (Its embryological origin is debated - traditionally taught as mesonephric-duct/mesodermal, but modern lineage-tracing suggests it is largely endodermal like the rest of the bladder.)

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: Which receptor/nerve promotes urine storage by relaxing the detrusor?
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: Sympathetic beta-3 receptors relax the detrusor (storage), while alpha-1 receptors contract the internal sphincter.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: Detrusor hypertrophy with wall trabeculation and diverticula in an older man most likely results from:
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: Chronic outflow obstruction (commonly BPH) forces the detrusor to hypertrophy, producing trabeculation and diverticula.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: Which layer/feature is characteristic of the bladder muscularis?
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: The detrusor consists of three interwoven (not distinctly separate) smooth-muscle layers.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: The external urethral sphincter is under voluntary control via the:
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: The somatic pudendal nerve provides voluntary control of the external urethral sphincter.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: Recurrent pyelonephritis and renal scarring in a child with an incompetent vesicoureteric junction is termed:
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: Vesicoureteric reflux allows infected urine to ascend, causing recurrent pyelonephritis and reflux nephropathy (scarring).

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: Which immunohistochemical panel best supports a urothelial origin for a poorly differentiated tumour?
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: CK7, CK20, GATA3 and uroplakin support urothelial differentiation; the other panels indicate lung, mesothelial, neuroendocrine and muscle lineages respectively.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: Which statement about urothelium is correct?
options: It is stratified with umbrella cells and adjusts thickness with distension
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: Urothelium is a stratified epithelium with characteristic umbrella cells and a variable apparent thickness that depends on the degree of distension.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: The single most important prognostic distinction in bladder cancer, dictating TURBT/BCG versus radical cystectomy, is:
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: Whether the tumour invades the muscularis propria (detrusor, >=T2) is the key prognostic/management split: non-muscle-invasive disease is treated with TURBT +/- intravesical BCG, whereas muscle-invasive disease usually needs radical cystectomy or chemoradiation.

histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.question: After a complete suprasacral spinal cord injury, loss of suprapontine inhibition of the sacral micturition reflex typically causes:
options: A spastic (reflex) neurogenic bladder with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia
Permanent retention with no reflex ever returning
Loss of all detrusor smooth muscle
histology__RENAL__Ureter & Bladder.explanation: The sacral (S2-4) micturition reflex is normally inhibited by higher centres via the pontine micturition centre; a suprasacral cord injury releases it, producing a spastic (reflex) neurogenic bladder, often with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia. A sacral cord/cauda equina lesion instead gives a flaccid, areflexic bladder.

histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.question: Which sequence correctly lists the renal arteries from largest to the afferent arteriole?
options: Renal -> segmental -> interlobar -> arcuate -> cortical radiate -> afferent
Renal -> arcuate -> interlobar -> cortical radiate -> afferent
Renal -> cortical radiate -> arcuate -> interlobar -> afferent
histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.explanation: The order is renal -> segmental -> interlobar (between pyramids) -> arcuate (over pyramid bases) -> cortical radiate/interlobular -> afferent arteriole.

histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.question: The arcuate arteries are found:
options: Arching over the bases of the pyramids at the corticomedullary junction
histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.explanation: Arcuate arteries arch over the pyramid bases at the corticomedullary junction — a key low-power landmark.

histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.question: The renal microcirculation is unusual because:
options: It drains into the hepatic portal vein
It has only a single capillary bed
Two capillary beds in series are bridged by the efferent arteriole (an arteriolar portal system)
histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.explanation: The renal microcirculation has two capillary beds in series - glomerular then peritubular/vasa recta - bridged by the efferent ARTERIOLE. This differs from classic portal systems (hepatic, hypophyseal), where the two capillary beds are bridged by a VEIN.

histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.question: The vasa recta primarily function to:
options: Preserve the medullary osmotic gradient as a countercurrent exchanger
histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.explanation: The vasa recta are passive countercurrent exchangers that supply the medulla while preserving its osmotic gradient; the loop of Henle builds the gradient.

histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.question: Which vessel gives rise to the second (reabsorptive) capillary bed?
histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.explanation: The efferent arteriole leaving the glomerulus supplies the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta — the low-pressure reabsorptive bed.

histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.question: The renal medulla is especially vulnerable to ischaemic injury because:
options: It is perfused only by the vasa recta and works on a marginal oxygen supply
It has a very high blood flow
It is supplied by end arteries directly
histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.explanation: The medulla is hypoxia-prone because countercurrent O2 exchange in the vasa recta short-circuits oxygen away from the deep medulla, while the thick ascending limb has a high O2 demand - so the S3 tubule and TAL of the outer medulla are hit first in ATN/papillary necrosis.

histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.question: A young woman with hypertension has a 'string of beads' appearance of the renal artery on angiography. The diagnosis is:
histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.explanation: Fibromuscular dysplasia causes the classic 'string of beads' renal artery appearance in young women and is a cause of renovascular hypertension.

histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.question: Occlusion of a segmental renal artery causes infarction because these arteries are:
options: End arteries with no collateral supply
histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.explanation: Renal segmental arteries are end arteries; occlusion produces a wedge-shaped infarct as there is no collateral flow.

histology__RENAL__Renal Vasculature.question: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis affecting BOTH the afferent and efferent arterioles is characteristic of:
